Question: Knowing what you know, what advice would you give your own children about choosing a long-term romantic partner?
Answer: The hunt for a long-term partner is much like the search for a habitable planet. There are billions of planets out there, plenty fish in the sea to choose from. What you are looking for, you will find. Jupiters? Sure. Saturns? No problem. Earths? Of course. But you’re not just looking for any old planet out there. Earth-like or not, some may be far too hot, others far too cold. Others may be on orbits that give them summers hotter than Venus and winters colder than Jupiter. Still others may come from a background that makes chemistry difficult. Think planets around O, B, A stars, or planets around M stars. You see, what you are looking for is quite specific. One not too hot, and one not too cold. One that has the chemistry to support liquid water, and more importantly, life. You see, the key word is chemistry. Where there is no chemistry, there is no chance. Just think. If Earth had the atmosphere of Jupiter, would we have a chance to be here today? No, of course not! If it were, perhaps we’d be living on Jupiter instead, but surprise surprise, that place is deader than a doorknob. But alas, one’s Jupiter may be another’s Earth, and vice versa. Point is, you have to put yourself out there to find those Earths. You see, with Kepler, the key word is patience. Kepler studies a small patch of the sky, and look how many fish it caught. The dating game is no different. Even in places where you don’t expect, there will be fish, there will be planets, there will be chances. You just have to be patient. Don’t force it, because no matter how beautiful or how amazing a person is, if the chemistry isn’t right, it will never be right. Don’t get me wrong. Saturn is perhaps the most beautiful object in the Solar System. But do we have a chance to find any life in its atmosphere? Probably not. Alas, do not despair if all you are finding is Jupiters and Saturns. The Earths are out there. It took us almost 20 years to find the first ones. But find them we did, and now, we know of hundreds of them. The dating game is no different. Whether one day or one thousand days, find an Earth you will, and when you do, the rest will be history. Never look back. It’s a numbers game. Look long enough, and you will find. Just be patient, and allow it to happen. Don’t force anything, because like I said, you wouldn’t want to live on a Jupiter or Saturn anyway.

Question: Can airplanes and jet fighters fly with no atmosphere?
Answer: First things first, all jet engines breathe air, so they will flame out due to lack of atmosphere. Furthermore, planes fly based on Bernoulli's principle of lift. The shape of the wing causes the air to move on top of the wing faster. This because in fluid dynamics, an increase in the speed of a fluid, causes a simultaneous decrease in the pressure of the fluid. This will cause the plane to climb, because objects in a fluid such as air like to go from high pressure areas to low pressure areas. You can observe the same effect by tying two soda cans slightly apart, and blowing air through the gap between the cans. Most would think the cans would fly apart, but due to Bernoulli's principle of lift, the cans are sucked together by the fast air moving through the gap. In the same sense, the aircraft is the soda can but on a much grander scale. The faster moving air on top of the airfoil will cause the plane to be sucked to the low pressure area. In the case of the plane, this means up, and the plane will achieve flight once the difference in pressure becomes greater than the pull of gravity on Earth. The net pull of all the forces acting on the plane is a pull towards the sky, and forwards due to the thrust being supplied. However, to generate the lift needed, you either need a really powerful wind, or a lot of thrust, hence the engine. Thrust is a huge part of the equation, and without thrust or some equivalent, you won't fly even in the atmosphere of Venus. Current jet engines such as the GE-90-115B or the CF6-50 breathe air, and flame out when faced with a lack of oxygen. If you could build a non-air breathing engine, powerful enough to power an object through the sky without the aid of an atmosphere, then this machine would be able to fly. This is how a rocket flies, because it has so much thrust that even though it looks nothing like an airplane should look, it is still able to fly because it has enough thrust. But I'm assuming your question only concerns commercial and fighter planes, not space planes.

Question: If WW3 got announced on the news and you had a plane and supplies, where would you take your family?
Answer: I would fly to one of the airstrips on the South Pole. Sure, it is remote. Sure, it is cold. But do I give a damn? I’m going to survive. It may be uncomfortable and take some time to get used to, but I’d take Amundsen-Scott Station over a concentration camp or something. I’d camp out there until the war was over. In the winter, I’d power up the APU inside the plane as heat, assuming I had fuel. If I didn’t have fuel, well I’d probably stay indoors somewhere, build an igloo or something. And if the world went to shit? I’d still be living happy as a hermit blissfully unaware of the shit that’s falling around me.

Question: How do parents deal with false (scientific) facts being taught to your child in school?
Answer: I’m no teacher, but myself having recently graduated high school, am somewhat qualified to answer this question. When I was in elementary school, I was attending an extremely religious-based school. Now, by religious, I mean that I was threatened with detention for wearing a Buddhist necklace my grandfather gave me. As such, science was not exactly the most accurate in that place. One incident that still irks me to this day happened during a writing workshop thingamabob they had us do in 3rd or 4th grade. Our assignment was to write a story about a fictional event based off a real-life event. Myself, being the aviation geek I am, decided to write a story based on the real event of Air Transat 236, an Airbus A330 aircraft that ran out of fuel over the ocean, eventually gliding more than 100 miles to a safe landing in the Azores. In my story, I used an Airbus A340 instead of an A330, and instead of a fuel leak, I decided to make it a calculation error like the Air Canada Gimli Glider incident. Last but not least, instead of a safe landing in the Azores, the A340 in my story would ditch in the rough choppy seas. If this sounds like a big project for a 10-year old, well, it was. I wrote about a page of this thing before realizing that I had my hands full and that I should probably ask my teacher for help. Now, when I showed my teacher the notes I’d scribbled for my outline and the page I had written, instead of getting the assistance I needed, I was chastised for not following the assignment guidelines, threatened with lunch detention, and sent to start over. My crime? My story, real as it was, was deemed, “too unrealistic to ever happen, too violent for the context of a 4th-grade classroom, and too gory for a good Christian mind.” When I protested to my teacher that this in fact really did happen, she shook her head, saying there was no way an airplane could continue flying after running out of fuel, especially over an ocean like Air Transat did. I tried explaining to her the concept of the airplane retaining momentum but she wouldn’t budge. Claiming quite adamantly I was wrong and had no clue what I was talking about, she even threatened me with a trip to the principal’s office for questioning her knowledge of physics rather rudely, justified as I felt I was. I pleaded with her one last time, promising I would allow everyone to live, but she wouldn't have it. Instead, as punishment for causing so much trouble, she assigned me a topic about “fairy-pixies,” since I was so adamant about writing a “fantasy piece.” Sullen and defeated, I returned to my seat in the computer lab and started typing out a half-assed story about fairy pixies. Or at least I was pretending to. In secret, I was actually researching the concept of glide ratio and technique of dead-stick landings. While I was reading the biography of Captain Robert Piche, I pledged that I would never allow myself to naively believe wrong facts like my teacher must have done at some point in her life. Whenever I had a doubt, I would research something. As a former US president once said, “Trust, but verify.” The trust part is optional, since people like my former teacher shouldn’t be trusted. But the verification part? Since even the smartest people make mistakes, verification is mandatory. The top scientists and statisticians would agree with me. Always verify and double-verify your findings. If you, or any of your friends should encounter wrong-fact preachers in school like I did, teach your kids the concept of “Trust but verify.” In other words, take the teacher’s words with a grain of salt until you verify what they are telling you is true. It will go a long way for them.

Question: Have you ever lost any respect for someone instantly?
